Ground. An arbitrary reference point in a circuit assigned zero volts, against which all other voltages are measured. Though sometimes called earth, especially in AC mains safety, ground in most electronics is a local reference plane or conductor, not a physical earth connection. All voltage measurements are relative; ground is the chosen zero.

Ground is fundamentally a reference, not an absolute. Every circuit voltage is measured relative to ground—the voltage at a node equals the voltage at that node minus the voltage at ground. A single-point ground with one return path minimizes noise loops. Multiple return paths at different frequencies create ground bounce and crosstalk. Star grounding connects all ground returns to a single point, preventing ground loops that couple noise into sensitive signals.

In alternating current power, earth ground—true Earth—is a safety requirement. A low-impedance return through the utility ground protects against shock and fire. Ground planes in printed circuit boards provide a low-impedance return path for current and act as shields for high-frequency noise.

Floating ground, where there is no connection to mains earth, is used in safety-isolated circuits. Ground is defined locally within the isolated domain. Common-mode voltage is the voltage of ground itself relative to mains earth. Circuits must either tolerate this offset or reject it via differential sensing. In analog circuits, ground noise—ripple on the return path—couples into signal paths and degrades dynamic range. For this reason, power and signal grounds may be separated near sensitive amplifiers.
